parts.intro: You will hear a woman at a community kitchen taking a booking from a man who wants to join a cooking course.

turns.text: Good morning, Hartfield Community Kitchen, this is Gemma speaking. How can I help?
Oh, hello. I'm calling about the evening cooking courses. I saw them advertised and I'd like to book a place, if there's still room.
Of course. Let me just open the booking form. Can I take your name first?
Yes, it's Tomas Brennick.
Could you spell the surname for me?
Sure. It's B-R-E-N-N-I-C-K. Brennick.
Thank you. And which course were you interested in? We have four running this term: baking, world street food, vegetarian cooking and cooking on a budget.

Well, I was going to ask about the baking one, but a friend told me it's mostly cakes, and I don't really have a sweet tooth. So I think I'll go for the vegetarian course instead. I'm trying to eat less meat.
Good choice, that's one of our most popular. Now, it runs on two evenings. The Tuesday group is completely full, I'm afraid, but there are still three places left in the Thursday group.
Thursday's fine. What time does it start?
Half past six, and it finishes at nine. The first session is on the fourteenth of March.
Great. And how much is it?
The standard price is 22 pounds a session, which covers all the ingredients. But if you live in the borough, there's a residents' rate of 18 pounds.
I do live locally, just off Mill Lane.
Then it's 18 for you. You'll just need to show something with your address on it on the first evening, like a utility bill.
No problem. Is there anything I need to bring?
We provide knives and all the equipment, but please bring an apron. Oh, and a container, a plastic box or something like that, because you'll usually want to take home what you've cooked.
Good idea, I'll remember that.
And just for our records, how did you hear about the course? Was it the poster in the library?
I did see a poster there, but that's not where I found it. It was the newsletter that comes through the door every month.
Lovely, thanks.
Er, could I ask a few things about the place itself? I've never been inside.

Sure. The building's a bit unusual, actually. It was a primary school until about fifteen years ago, and the kitchen is in what used to be the school hall. People often think it was a church because of the tall windows, but no, it was definitely a school.
Is there parking?
There's a small car park at the back, but it fills up quickly, so the bus is easier if you can manage it.
I'll probably cycle anyway. And how many people are in each group?

A maximum of ten. Some people assume that's because of insurance, but really it's because we only have ten cooking stations, and we want everyone to have their own space and equipment rather than sharing.
That makes sense. I'm a complete beginner, by the way. Is that a problem?

Not at all, most people are beginners. What we do need, though, before the first class, is to know about any food allergies, because the teacher orders the ingredients a week in advance. We don't need your phone number, because the system's already saved it from this call.
Right. Well, I'm allergic to peanuts, actually.
Okay, I'll make a note of that now, so you don't need to email us. Now, how would you like to pay? Most people pay online by card, but we also accept bank transfers.
Could I just pay in cash on the first evening?
I'm afraid we stopped taking cash last year.
Oh, okay. Then I'll do it online. I'll pay by card on your website tonight.
Perfect. That's everything, then. We'll send a confirmation once your payment comes through. See you on the fourteenth!

parts.intro: You will hear a guide talking to a group of visitors at the start of a tour of a restored river port.

turns.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Port Callow. My name's Rhys and I'll be your guide this morning. Before we set off, let me give you a little background. People often assume the port was at its busiest in the early 1700s, when the first stone quay was built, but in fact trade really peaked in the mid-1800s, when steamers carried wool and timber down the river to the coast. By the 1920s the railway had taken most of that trade away, and the port slowly fell into ruin.

The restoration began about twelve years ago. The city council did contribute a small grant, and a few local businesses donated materials, but the bulk of the money, around eighty per cent, came from a public fund-raising campaign. Thousands of ordinary people bought a single brick with their name on it, and you'll see those bricks along the main wharf.

Now, a couple of quick requests. You're welcome to take photos anywhere, and you can touch the old boats on display; they're very solid. But please keep to the marked paths, because some of the old timber decking is still being repaired. And you don't need to stay right beside me the whole time. If you fall behind, just follow the blue signs.

One more thing about your ticket. It doesn't include the boat trip, I'm afraid, that's sold separately at the ferry office, and there's no lunch included either. But the good news is that you can come back and use the same ticket any time within seven days.

Finally, you may have noticed the old toll gate at the entrance where you came in. That's the original gate. For many years it was kept in the museum in town, but it was brought back here last year, and it's now where we start and finish every tour. So if you lose the group, wait there.

Right, let's look at the map and I'll tell you about the five places we'll visit. First, the Customs House. This is where ships' cargoes were checked and taxed. Today the ground floor holds a collection of old charts and maps of the river, some of them over two hundred years old. People sometimes expect a restaurant here, because of the lovely terrace, but the restaurant is actually somewhere else. I'll come to that.

Next is the Rope Walk, a long, narrow building, almost two hundred metres long, where ropes for the ships were made. A team of volunteers gives demonstrations, and they'll let you have a go at twisting your own piece of rope to take home.

Then we'll climb up to Crane Wharf. The giant steam crane itself doesn't work any more, but from the platform at the top you get the finest view of the river anywhere in Port Callow. On a clear day you can see all the way to the estuary.

After that comes Warehouse Row. These five brick warehouses once stored wool. Two of them are now artists' studios, and the largest has been turned into a seafood restaurant, which I can highly recommend.

And finally, the Ferry Steps. When the restoration team started work, the steps had almost completely collapsed. Luckily, the original engineer's drawings had survived in the city archive, so the steps were rebuilt exactly as they were in 1862. Now, you may have heard that the little ferry is free for children. That used to be true, but sadly it isn't any more. The ferry office is open as usual today, by the way, so you can buy boat tickets there. Okay, let's go.

parts.intro: You will hear two students, Mia and Jonah, discussing their survey on campus food waste with their tutor.

turns.text: Come in, Mia, Jonah. So, you wanted to talk about your survey project on food waste in the campus canteens.
Yes, thanks, Dr Varga. We've changed the plan quite a bit since the proposal.
Before we get to that, remind me why you chose food waste in the first place.

Well, partly because the student union has been campaigning about it, and we'd had a lecture on sustainability too. But honestly, the main reason was something we saw ourselves. We both work part-time in the main canteen, and we were shocked at how many full plates come back at the end of lunch.
Yes, it was really seeing it every day that made us want to investigate.

Personal experience is a good starting point. Now, I did read your first proposal. The question itself was clear enough, but it tried to cover all six food outlets on campus, and I felt that was far too ambitious for an eight-week project.
We agree now. So we've decided to focus on just one.
Which one?

We thought about the coffee bar in the library, because it's small and easy to observe, but it mostly sells drinks, so there isn't much food waste. And the Hilltop Cafe closes during the exam period, which is right in the middle of our data collection. So we're going with the Riverside canteen. It's the largest, and it serves hot meals at lunch and dinner.
Sensible. What about your sample? How many students are you hoping to reach?
We originally said five hundred responses to the questionnaire.
And do you think that's realistic?
It might be, actually. Our worry is less about the number and more about who answers. If we just put a link on the union website, we'll only hear from students who already care about the environment.
Exactly. That's the real risk, a biased sample rather than a small one. So how will you deal with it?
We're thinking of handing out cards with a QR code at the tills, so everyone who buys a meal gets one.
Good. And at the end of the project, what will you produce?

The department wants a written report, of course, but we'd also like to give a short presentation to the catering staff. We won't show them all the statistics, just a set of practical recommendations.
I like that. Recommendations will be far more useful to them than tables of numbers. Now, let's go through your methods one by one. The online questionnaire first.
We tested it on some friends and it took nearly fifteen minutes. People will give up halfway. So we're cutting it down to ten questions.
Good. And weighing the food left on plates?
That's the most important one, really. But we can't just walk into the kitchen with a set of scales. Mrs Dorrell, the catering manager, has to agree first, so I'm emailing her today.
What about the interviews with kitchen staff?
We'll do those before anything else, actually, in week one, because what the staff tell us will help us decide what to weigh.
And photographing the trays?

We did think about combining the photos with the weighing, but some students might object to being photographed, even if it's only their tray, and the pictures are slow to analyse. So we've decided to leave it out altogether.
Fair enough. And the bin audit, going through what's thrown away at the end of the day?
We're not sure we've designed the categories properly: fruit, bread, cooked meals and so on. Could you look at our category list before we begin?
Of course. Send it to me by Friday and I'll comment on it.

parts.intro: You will hear part of a biology lecture about how desert ants find their way.

turns.text: Good morning. Today I want to look at one of the most impressive navigators in the animal kingdom, and it isn't a bird or a whale. It's the desert ant. Several species of these ants live in hot, flat deserts, where there are very few features to help them find their way, and yet a single ant can wander more than a hundred metres from its nest in search of food and then return in an almost perfectly straight line.

Let's start with their daily routine, which is rather surprising. Most insects avoid the midday sun, but desert ants do the opposite. They forage at the hottest time of the day, when the ground can reach sixty degrees. The reason is that this is when their predators, mainly lizards, are inactive, sheltering from the heat. The ants feed largely on other insects that have died of heat exhaustion, so the hottest hours are both the safest and the most productive. Of course, the cost is that every minute outside is dangerous, which is why returning home quickly matters so much.

So how do they do it? The main strategy is known as path integration. As the ant moves, twisting and turning on its outward journey, it constantly keeps track of two things: the direction it is travelling in and the distance it has covered. By combining these, it always knows, roughly, where its nest lies relative to its current position, and it can head straight back.

Take direction first. You might expect the ant to use the sun itself, and it does to some extent, but more importantly it reads the pattern of polarised light in the sky. Sunlight becomes polarised as it is scattered in the atmosphere, and this creates a pattern across the sky that humans cannot see but ants can, using special cells at the top of their eyes. Even when the sun is hidden, a small patch of blue sky is enough.

Distance is more puzzling, and for a long time researchers assumed the ants simply estimated how long they had been walking. In fact, they count their steps. This was shown in a rather elegant experiment. Researchers trained ants to walk to a feeder, and then, at the feeder, they changed the length of some of the ants' legs. Some ants had their legs shortened, while others had their legs lengthened by attaching tiny stilts made from bristles. When the ants set off home, those on stilts took longer strides and so walked too far, overshooting the nest, while those with shorter legs stopped too soon. The ants were clearly relying on the number of steps, not on time.

Path integration is powerful, but small errors build up over a long journey. So, when the ant gets close to home, it switches to other cues. Desert ants learn visual landmarks, such as rocks and small shrubs, around the nest entrance, and they store something like a snapshot of the scene. They also use smell. The nest has a distinctive odour, which is carried by the wind, and an ant that is slightly off course will often turn and walk upwind until it picks up the scent.

One more remarkable detail. When an ant finds a large piece of food, it often has to drag it, which means walking backwards. For years it was thought this would confuse the navigation system, but recent work shows that the ants still keep their course while walking backwards, occasionally putting the food down to turn round and check the view before carrying on.

Finally, why does any of this matter beyond biology? Engineers are increasingly interested in how such a tiny brain, smaller than a pinhead, manages such reliable navigation with so little energy. Designers of robots that must operate where satellite signals fail, for instance inside buildings, underground or on other planets, have already built prototypes that use a polarised light compass and step counting inspired by the ant. Next week we'll look at how honeybees communicate the location of food.

passages.title: Bending the Light: A Short History of Lighthouse Lenses
passages.text:
For most of human history, a lighthouse was little more than a fire on a hill. The earliest coastal lights burned wood or coal in open iron baskets, and their glow was weak, smoky and unreliable. On a clear night a coal fire might be seen from perhaps eight kilometres away; in rain or fog, sailors could pass close to the shore without noticing it at all. Keepers struggled to keep the flames alive in strong winds, and much of the light that was produced simply escaped upwards into the sky, where it was of no use to anyone at sea.

The first major improvement came in the late eighteenth century, when oil lamps with glass chimneys began to replace open fires. These lamps burned more cleanly, but on their own they were still not bright enough. Engineers therefore placed polished metal reflectors behind the flames. Shaped like shallow bowls, the reflectors gathered light that would otherwise have been lost and sent it out in a single direction. A large lighthouse might use twenty or more lamps, each with its own reflector, arranged on a frame. The system worked, but it had serious weaknesses. The reflectors were usually made of copper coated with silver, and the silver tarnished quickly in the salty air, so keepers had to spend hours each day polishing them. Even when perfectly clean, the reflectors absorbed roughly half of the light that fell on them.

An obvious alternative was to use a lens, which bends light rather than bouncing it back. However, a conventional lens large enough to gather the light of a lighthouse lamp would have had to be enormously thick in the centre. Such a lens would be extremely heavy, and thick glass of that period was often full of bubbles and impurities that absorbed light. It might also crack as it heated up during the night. For these reasons, early experiments with solid lenses were disappointing, and most lighthouse authorities stayed loyal to reflectors.

The breakthrough came in the 1820s, when a French physicist proposed a radically different design. He realised that only the curved surface of a lens actually bends light; the glass behind that surface merely adds weight. His solution was to divide the lens into a series of concentric rings, each one a thin slice of the curve that a solid lens would have had. Viewed from the side, the lens looked stepped, rather like a flight of stairs. Because the rings were thin, the whole lens used far less glass, weighed much less and lost far less light. Around the central rings he added glass prisms, which caught light escaping above and below the lamp and redirected it towards the horizon.

The results were dramatic. A lighthouse fitted with one of the new stepped lenses could be seen from more than thirty kilometres away, and it needed only a single lamp instead of dozens. Within a few decades, lighthouse authorities in many countries had adopted the design. The lenses were manufactured in several standard sizes, known as orders. The largest, the first order, stood taller than a person and was used on major coastal headlands, while smaller orders served harbours, piers and rivers.

Making these lenses demanded great skill. Each prism had to be ground and polished by hand to exactly the right angle, and then fixed into a heavy frame made of bronze, a metal chosen because it resists corrosion by sea air. A large lens might contain more than a thousand separate pieces of glass, and building one could take several years. For much of the nineteenth century, only a handful of workshops in Europe were capable of producing them, and their lenses were shipped to lighthouses all over the world.

Lighthouses also needed to be recognised. A sailor who saw a light needed to know which lighthouse it was, and therefore where the ship was. To solve this problem, engineers gave each light its own pattern of flashes. Some lenses were made in separate panels and rotated around the lamp, producing a beam that swept across the sea like the hand of a clock. At first the heavy lenses were turned by clockwork, which the keeper had to wind every few hours throughout the night. Later, the entire lens was floated on a bath of mercury, which allowed a lens weighing several tonnes to be turned by a very small force.

In the twentieth century, electric lamps replaced oil, and the role of the keeper gradually disappeared as lighthouses were automated. More recently, many of the great glass lenses have been removed and replaced by small, low-maintenance electronic units. Satellite navigation means that ships rely far less on lighthouses than they once did. Yet many of the old lenses survive in museums, where visitors still admire them both as practical inventions and as objects of remarkable beauty.

passages.title: Cooling the City: Urban Heat Islands and Cool Roofs
passages.text:
A  On a still summer evening, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside only a short drive away. This effect, known as the urban heat island, was first described in the nineteenth century by amateur weather observers who noticed that thermometers in town gardens regularly read higher than those in nearby villages. Today, with more than half of the world's population living in cities, it has become a serious concern for planners, doctors and energy companies alike.

B  The causes are well understood. Natural surfaces such as soil, grass and trees stay relatively cool because they hold water, and the evaporation of that water absorbs heat. Cities replace these surfaces with asphalt, concrete and brick, which are dry and often dark. Dark materials absorb a large proportion of the sunlight that strikes them, and dense materials store that heat during the day and release it slowly after sunset. This is why the difference between city and countryside is usually greatest at night rather than in the afternoon. Tall buildings make matters worse by trapping heat in narrow streets and blocking the breezes that might otherwise carry it away, while vehicles, air-conditioners and factories add heat of their own.

C  The consequences reach well beyond discomfort. During heatwaves, death rates rise sharply in cities, particularly among elderly people and those with heart or lung conditions, and warm nights are especially dangerous because the body gets no chance to recover. Higher temperatures also speed up the chemical reactions that produce ground-level ozone, worsening air quality. And as people turn up their air-conditioning, demand for electricity peaks, which can overload power networks and, where electricity comes from fossil fuels, add to the very greenhouse gases that are warming the planet in the long term. In this way the problem feeds on itself.

D  Among the many proposed responses, one of the simplest is to change the colour of the city's roofs. Roofs make up roughly a fifth of the surface area of a typical city, and many are covered in dark materials such as bitumen or black rubber. A conventional dark roof may reflect only five to ten per cent of the sunlight that hits it, and on a hot afternoon its surface can reach eighty degrees Celsius. A so-called cool roof, coated with a white or specially formulated reflective material, may reflect seventy per cent or more, and its surface stays only a little warmer than the surrounding air. Because less heat passes into the building below, the rooms under the roof stay cooler too.

E  The benefits have been measured in a number of field trials. In a three-year trial in the southern city of Valmora, researchers painted the roofs of forty single-storey houses white and compared them with similar unpainted houses in the same streets. Indoor temperatures in the painted homes were on average two degrees lower on summer afternoons, and the households that used air-conditioning reduced their cooling bills by around fifteen per cent. Computer models suggest that if most roofs in a city were converted, average air temperatures across the whole urban area could fall by as much as one degree, a modest figure, but one that could make a real difference on the most extreme days.

F  Cool roofs are not without drawbacks, however. In cities with cold winters, a reflective roof also reflects the weak winter sunshine, so buildings may need slightly more heating. In most climates this so-called winter penalty is smaller than the summer savings, but that is not true everywhere. White surfaces also become dirty, and a coating that loses its brightness loses much of its effect, so roofs need regular cleaning or recoating. Some residents object to the glare from bright roofs, especially those living in taller buildings that look down on them. And roofs are only part of the picture: they do little to cool the street where pedestrians actually walk.

G  For this reason, most specialists see cool roofs as one tool among several. Planting street trees provides shade and cools the air through evaporation; green roofs covered in plants offer insulation and absorb rainwater as well as heat; and paler paving can reduce surface temperatures at ground level. Some cities now require reflective materials on all new flat roofs, while others offer grants to owners who convert existing ones. What experts broadly agree on is that the cost of acting is low compared with the cost of doing nothing, as heatwaves become more frequent and more intense.

passages.title: The Uses of an Empty Hour
passages.text:
Few experiences are as widely disliked as boredom. We fidget in queues, reach for our phones the moment a conversation stalls and fill every spare minute with podcasts, messages and short videos. Technology companies have built extraordinarily profitable businesses on our apparent determination never to be bored again. Yet in recent years a counter-argument has gained popularity, in magazines and self-help books as much as in academic journals: boredom, we are told, is not an enemy but a hidden resource, the soil from which original ideas grow. If we eliminate it, the argument runs, we risk eliminating creativity too. The claim is attractive, but I believe it deserves far more scrutiny than it usually receives.

The case for boredom rests largely on a well-known experiment. The psychologist Imogen Taverly asked one group of volunteers to spend fifteen minutes copying numbers from a telephone directory, a deliberately tedious task, while a control group went straight to the main test. Both groups were then asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. The bored volunteers produced more ideas, and their ideas were judged to be more unusual. Taverly concluded that boredom pushes the mind to seek stimulation elsewhere, and that this restless searching makes unexpected connections more likely.

I do not doubt the finding, but I am wary of how far it has been stretched. The experiment measured a narrow skill, generating ideas quickly in a laboratory, and it measured it within minutes of a mildly dull activity. Real creative work, whether it is writing a novel or designing a bridge, involves long periods of focused and often frustrating effort, and it is not at all obvious that fifteen minutes of copying numbers tells us much about it. Moreover, later attempts to repeat the study have produced mixed results. A team led by Rafael Ondieki found the effect only when participants had also been told that their creativity was being assessed, which suggests that motivation, rather than boredom itself, may have done much of the work.

There is also an important distinction that popular accounts tend to blur. Researchers increasingly separate boredom from mind-wandering, the drifting of attention away from the task at hand. Mind-wandering can occur when we are bored, but it also happens during pleasant, undemanding activities such as walking, showering or gardening, and these states seem far more reliably linked to creative insight. Hana Leskovar, who studies daydreaming, argues that what matters is not the unpleasant feeling of boredom but the freedom it occasionally gives the mind to roam. On this view, boredom is at best an inefficient route to a state that can be reached in more agreeable ways.

Boredom also has a darker side that its enthusiasts rarely mention. People who are frequently bored are more likely to report anxiety and low mood, and in some studies bored participants chose to give themselves mild electric shocks rather than sit alone with their thoughts. Chronic boredom at school is associated with lower achievement, not higher, and boredom at work is a common reason for leaving a job. To present boredom as something to be welcomed, without acknowledging these associations, seems to me irresponsible.

None of this means that the critics of constant stimulation are wrong. There is good evidence that the habit of checking a phone whenever attention flags can make it harder to concentrate, and some evidence that it reduces the time we spend reflecting on our own experiences. Gideon Marr, a sociologist, has shown that adults who described their days as always full were less likely to report having had a new idea in the previous month. But notice what this finding actually implies. The problem is not a shortage of boredom; it is a shortage of unstructured time. A person who takes an hour-long walk without headphones has not been bored, yet they have given their mind exactly the space that boredom is supposed to provide.

Why, then, has the idea of useful boredom proved so appealing? Part of the answer, I suspect, is that it offers a comforting story. It reassures parents that children who complain of having nothing to do are not being neglected but nurtured, and it tells adults who feel overwhelmed by their devices that the cure is simple and free. Comforting stories are not necessarily false, but they deserve particular caution precisely because we want to believe them.

What should we conclude? Boredom is best understood as a signal rather than a gift: a message that our current activity is failing to engage us. Sometimes the right response is to let our thoughts drift; sometimes it is to change what we are doing. The creative benefit, where it exists, comes from what we do with the signal, not from the discomfort itself. Rather than seeking boredom, we might do better to protect periods of quiet, undirected activity, and to treat a child's boredom as an invitation to explore rather than as a virtue in its own right.
